summary: Relaxes the IANA allocation rules for the Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access (PANA), making it easier to register new values. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: It makes it easier to add new entries to a shared list used by a network sign-in system.

subtitle: Relaxed registration rules for the network access authentication protocol.

tldr.problem: The PANA protocol (RFC 5191) had strict IANA allocation rules that made it difficult to assign new values for experimental or special-case extensions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5872 updates the allocation rules to allow both IETF Review and IESG Approval for several PANA namespaces, giving the steering group flexibility to assign values in exceptional cases.
tldr.outcome: Experimental extensions and special allocations can be approved without waiting for full IETF consensus, speeding up the evolution of PANA.

facts.label: Affected namespaces
facts.value: 5 (Message Types, Flags, AVP Flags, Result-Code, Termination-Cause)

today: RFC 5872 is a standards-track specification that updates RFC 5191. It is currently active and allows IESG Approval for PANA allocations.

sections.title: Making Room for Extensions
sections.content:
PANA (Protocol for Carrying Authentication for Network Access) is used when a device first connects to a network and needs to prove its identity. RFC 5191 defined the protocol and set strict rules for registering new message types, flags, and result codes.

The original rules required full IETF Review for most new allocations. RFC 5872 relaxes these rules to allow the Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) to approve allocations under special circumstances, such as supporting an experimental extension or a protocol variant that deserves registration even though it does not meet the default criteria.
sections.eli5: The original protocol was very strict about adding new features. This makes it easier to try new ideas.

sections.title: What Changed
sections.content:
The update affects five PANA namespaces: Message Types, Message Flags, AVP Flags, Result-Code values, and Termination-Cause values. For each, the allocation rule is changed from IETF Review only to allow either IETF Review or IESG Approval.

The ranges remain the same (for example, values 1 through 4 for Message Types were defined in RFC 5191). The change is only in how new values in the remaining ranges are assigned.
sections.eli5: Five different lists of codes and flags now have two ways to get new entries instead of one.

sections.title: Experimental Values
sections.content:
PANA defines a range of values (65,520 to 65,535 for Message Types) reserved for experimental messages. These codes are for testing only, and no guarantee is made that experimental messages will interoperate between different implementations.

The RFC notes that when deploying experimental values across networks, potential harmful side effects must be carefully evaluated. Guidance from RFC 3692 about experimental code points should be followed.
sections.eli5: Some code numbers are set aside just for trying out new ideas. These are not for production use.
